Abstract

Low-bit inference on accelerators with native 4-bit support requires quantizing both weights and activations to realize the full throughput gains these formats provide. While post-training weight quantization has been extensively studied, activation quantization remains considerably more challenging and typically requires calibration data. In this work, we introduce DualQuant, a dual-scale, calibration-free post-training quantization framework that directly minimizes the weight-reconstruction Mean Squared Error (MSE) and, as an immediate by-product, yields per-channel activation rescalings prior to activation quantization. Our key observation is that the scaling factors obtained by minimizing weight-reconstruction error also provide effective activation rescalings, enabling competitive activation quantization without calibration data. We formulate DualQuant as a non-differentiable weight-reconstruction problem and develop an efficient solver based on variable splitting and block coordinate descent, where each subproblem admits a closed-form update. By treating the quantizer as a black box and projecting scales onto their format-specific admissible set after each update, DualQuant provides a unified algorithm supporting a wide range of formats, including INT4, INT8, the full MX family, and NVFP4. To our knowledge, DualQuant is the first dual-scaling method to formally support MX and NV block formats. Across Llama and Qwen models evaluated on WikiText-2, C4, and zero-shot downstream tasks, DualQuant matches or exceeds the accuracy of calibration-based SmoothQuant across most models and formats, and substantially outperforms calibration-free baselines, with particularly large gains for MX and NV block formats. We further validate these gains with a real packed W4A4 inference path for Llama-3.1-8B on an RTX 4090. The resulting implementation closely matches the accuracy of fake quantization while delivering up to memory reduction and up to throughput speedup over BF16. Our anonymized codebase is available here.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have grown rapidly in scale, from dense models (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025) to mixture-of-experts architectures exceeding a trillion parameters (DeepSeek-AI, 2024; Jiang et al., 2024), placing enormous pressure on memory and compute at inference time. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) addresses this by compressing weights, activations, and KV-cache to low-bit representations without retraining. Modern accelerators such as NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs provide native 4-bit matrix multiplication (Rouhani et al., 2023; NVIDIA, 2025) delivering up to the throughput of FP16, but realizing this gain requires both weights and activations in a low-bit format. The central obstacle is that activation tensors exhibit systematic large-magnitude outliers in specific channels (Dettmers et al., 2022; Bondarenko et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2024) that dominate the quantization grid. Calibration-based methods address activation quantization effectively but require representative data, introducing distribution sensitivity and data-access overhead prohibitive in privacy-sensitive or on-device settings. This includes both scale-based approaches such as SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) and rotation-based approaches such as SpinQuant (Liu et al., 2025), which optimizes rotation matrices using calibration data. Calibration-free rotation-based methods such as QuaRot (Ashkboos et al., 2024) avoid this dependency but do not target activation-quantization error. In other words, no prior method achieves competitive calibration-free joint Weight and Activation (W+A) quantization across modern MX and NV formats.

In this work, we introduce DualQuant, a calibration-free dual-scale (per-row and per-column) PTQ framework that jointly quantizes weights and activations without any access to calibration data or activation statistics. The key insight is that channels with large-magnitude weight columns contribute disproportionately to the layer output and, as shown empirically, concentrate activation outliers (Sun et al., 2024; Dettmers et al., 2022; Bondarenko et al., 2021). Consequently, the column scales that minimize weight-reconstruction MSE attenuate these same channels, so they not only quantize the weights well but also implicitly define activation rescalings that we observe to substantially improve activation quantization—playing a role similar to SmoothQuant’s calibrated scales (Xiao et al., 2023), yet derived from weights alone. DualQuant obtains these row and column scales via Block Coordinate Descent (BCD) with closed-form updates and provable convergence guarantees (Tseng, 2001; Razaviyayn et al., 2013), treating the quantizer as a black-box operator and projecting scales to their admissible format set after each update, yielding a single unified algorithm that operates across INT4, MXINT4, MXFP4, and NVFP4. Evaluation on Qwen and Llama families confirms that DualQuant matches or surpasses SmoothQuant on W+A quantization across most formats and models, without any calibration data. Our main contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We formalize dual-scale weight quantization as a constrained non-convex optimization problem and solve it via BCD with closed-form per-coordinate updates, format-aware scale projection, and provable convergence guarantees, requiring no inner loop, no Hessian, and no calibration data. The same algorithm operates uniformly across INT4, MXINT4, MXFP4, and NVFP4, making DualQuant the first dual-scaling method that formally supports the full MX and NV formats.

  2. 2.

    We show that the column scales obtained from weight MSE minimization also serve as effective activation rescalings, enabling joint W+A quantization without any access to calibration data. Across Qwen and Llama families and four 4-bit formats, DualQuant closely matches or surpasses calibration-based SmoothQuant and significantly outperforms calibration-free baselines QuaRot and SINQ+, with especially large margins on MX and NV block data formats.

  3. 3.

    We validate DualQuant through a real packed W4A4 deployment of Llama-3.1-8B on an RTX 4090. The packed implementation matches fake-quantization accuracy to within perplexity on WikiText-2 while reducing memory usage by – and improving end-to-end speed by – over BF16. Incorporating the scales into the activation-quantization kernel avoids additional kernel launches and limits the quantization overhead to - of total GPU time.

5 Experiments

5.1 Joint weight-and-activation quantization

Table 1 reports joint W+A quantization perplexity on the Llama family across four 4-bit formats. DualQuant consistently matches or surpasses the calibration-based SmoothQuant, while requiring no calibration data. On MXFP4, DualQuant improves over SmoothQuant on WikiText-2 for all three models, substantially on Llama-2-7B and Llama-3.2-1B and narrowly on Llama-3.1-8B; on C4 the same holds except for Llama-3.1-8B, where DualQuant trails slightly. On MXINT4, DualQuant is better than SmoothQuant across both WikiText-2 and C4 for all three models. On INT4, DualQuant surpasses both SmoothQuant and AWQ+ across all models, demonstrating that weight-derived scales provide effective activation rescaling even on the standard integer format. On NVFP4, DualQuant achieves the strongest results among all methods on Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.2-1B, with the same overall trend on C4. In contrast, both calibration-free baselines degrade substantially on MX and NV formats: SINQ+ degrades on MXINT4 and MXFP4 and diverges completely on NVFP4, as its format-unaware scales fall outside the FP8 representable range; QuaRot similarly diverges on NVFP4 and degrades substantially on MX formats, as its Hadamard rotation redistributes activation magnitude in a way incompatible with block floating-point scaling. DualQuant avoids both failure modes by design, incorporating format constraints directly into the optimization and requiring no rotation or calibration data. Corresponding results on the Qwen family (Table 7, Appendix G) show consistent trends.11 1 The DualQuant–SINQ+ gap persists without our extensions: in SINQ’s native weight-only INT4 setting, DualQuant is more accurate on three of four models (Appendix H), so it stems from the objective itself.
